cards.statement: An interface accepts a class instance by matching members rather than an `implements` declaration.
cards.explanation: TypeScript compares the instance's members with the interface's required members. The class need not declare that it implements the interface.

cards.statement: `const p: { x: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 }` passes TypeScript's excess property check.
cards.explanation: The fresh literal has an unknown `y` property, so assignment to `{ x: number }` produces an excess property error.
cards.misconception: Structural assignment permits extra fields on fresh object literals just as it does on existing variables.

cards.statement: TypeScript rejects assigning a `{ readonly x: number }` value to a variable of type `{ x: number }`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript ignores `readonly` when comparing object property compatibility. An alias with a mutable property may therefore change the same object.
cards.misconception: The readonly modifier makes structurally identical object types assignment-incompatible.

cards.statement: `(a: number) => void` is assignable to the type `(a: number, b: string) => void`.
cards.explanation: A function may ignore extra arguments, so a source with fewer parameters fits a target with more, provided each of its parameters matches the target parameter in the same position.

cards.statement: Different parameter names make otherwise matching function signatures incompatible.
cards.explanation: Function compatibility compares parameter types and positions, not parameter names. `(a: number) => void` and `(b: number) => void` match.
cards.misconception: Parameter identifiers participate in function type compatibility.

cards.statement: Given `let f = () => ({ a: 1, b: 2 })`, TypeScript accepts assigning `f` to a `() => { a: number }` variable.
cards.explanation: TypeScript requires the source function's return type to be a subtype of the target's, and `{ a: number; b: number }` has every member that `{ a: number }` needs.

cards.statement: Unrelated classes with identically named private members are assignment-compatible.
cards.explanation: For a private member in the target, the corresponding source member must originate from the same class declaration. Matching names in unrelated classes do not suffice.
cards.misconception: Private members follow the same name-and-type structural rule as public members.

cards.statement: Class compatibility directly compares instance members even when constructors differ.
cards.explanation: When TypeScript compares class instance types, constructor signatures belong to the static side and do not affect instance compatibility.

cards.statement: Type annotations disappear from the JavaScript that TypeScript emits.
cards.explanation: TypeScript erases type annotations during compilation. They guide static checking but create no runtime type checks in the emitted JavaScript.

cards.statement: A value of type `any` can be assigned to a variable of type `never`.
cards.explanation: Even `any` is rejected as a source for `never`. Under assignment compatibility, `never` accepts only `never`.
cards.misconception: The escape hatch provided by any includes assignment to never.

cards.statement: A value of type `unknown` permits an arbitrary property call before narrowing.
cards.explanation: The checker rejects a property call on `unknown` until a check or assertion establishes a usable type.
cards.misconception: Unknown permits unchecked operations because it accepts values of any type.

cards.statement: A value of type `unknown` is directly assignable to a `string` variable.
cards.explanation: `unknown` is not assignable to `string` as-is. The value needs narrowing or a type assertion before that assignment.
cards.misconception: Because unknown can contain a string, it is assignable to string.

cards.statement: A value of type `never` is assignable to a `string` variable.
cards.explanation: `never` is assignable to every type, including `string`. It represents a value that cannot occur on a reachable path.

cards.statement: `undefined` is directly assignable to `void` with `strictNullChecks` enabled.
cards.explanation: The assignability table permits `undefined` as a source for `void` even when `strictNullChecks` is on.

cards.statement: TypeScript accepts `let n: number = done()` when `done` has the return type `void`.
cards.explanation: Apart from `void` itself, a `void` value is assignable only to `any` and `unknown`, whatever the `strictNullChecks` setting, so a void call result is unusable as a number.
cards.misconception: A void result can be assigned to a concrete value type such as number.

cards.statement: With `noImplicitAny` disabled, an uninferred parameter gets type `unknown`.
cards.explanation: An unannotated parameter with no inferred type falls back to `any`. Disabling `noImplicitAny` suppresses the error about that fallback.
cards.misconception: Turning off noImplicitAny replaces implicit any with unknown.

cards.statement: A remaining union case triggers an error when assigned to `never` in an exhaustive switch.
cards.explanation: An unhandled variant retains its own type in the remaining branch. Assigning it to `never` reports that the switch is incomplete.

cards.statement: A callback typed to return `void` may implement its body with a returned value.
cards.explanation: A function assigned to a `() => void` slot may return a value; callers using that slot ignore the result. This differs from explicitly annotating a function declaration with `: void`.

cards.statement: An unannotated array of sibling subclasses infers their shared base as its element type.
cards.explanation: When no candidate element type is a supertype of the others, best common type inference produces an array of their union rather than inventing an absent base type.
cards.misconception: Best common type inference searches the inheritance tree for a shared base even when it is absent from the candidates.

cards.statement: TypeScript flags `n` as implicit `any` in `xs.map(n => n.toFixed())` for `xs: number[]`.
cards.explanation: The callback sits where the signature of `map` supplies a contextual type, so TypeScript infers `n` as `number` and `noImplicitAny` has nothing to report.
cards.misconception: Unannotated callback parameters fall back to implicit any.

cards.statement: `let mode = 'open'` infers `mode` as `string` rather than the literal type.
cards.explanation: A `let` binding can later receive another string, so TypeScript widens the initializer's string literal type to `string`.

cards.statement: In `const opts = { retries: 3 }`, TypeScript infers `opts.retries` as the type `number`.
cards.explanation: A `const` binding only stops reassignment of `opts`. Its properties stay writable, so TypeScript widens the literal `3` to `number`.

cards.statement: `[1, 2] as const` receives a `readonly [1, 2]` tuple type.
cards.explanation: A const assertion retains the element literal types and infers an array literal as a readonly tuple.

cards.statement: `satisfies` replaces an expression's inferred type with the target type.
cards.explanation: `satisfies` checks compatibility with a target type while retaining the expression's resulting type. A type annotation gives the variable the annotated type.
cards.misconception: Satisfies changes the resulting type in the same way as a variable annotation.

cards.statement: A fresh `{ a: 1, b: 2 } satisfies Record<'a', number>` expression passes checking.
cards.explanation: The fresh object has an extra `b` key outside `Record<'a', number>`, so `satisfies` reports an error.
cards.misconception: Satisfies checks value types but overlooks unexpected object keys.

cards.statement: A double assertion through `unknown` bridges types that lack direct overlap.
cards.explanation: TypeScript rejects some direct assertions between unrelated types. Asserting first to `unknown` and then to the target type bypasses that overlap restriction.

cards.statement: The postfix `!` throws when its expression evaluates to `null`.
cards.explanation: Postfix `!` removes `null` and `undefined` from the expression's checked type but emits no runtime guard. The operator itself does not throw.
cards.misconception: The non-null assertion operator checks and rejects null at runtime.

cards.statement: Inside `typeof value === 'string'`, a `string | number` value narrows to `string`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript recognizes a `typeof` comparison as a type guard and removes the `number` branch inside the string case.

cards.statement: `typeof v === 'object'` narrows a value `v: object | null` to `object`.
cards.explanation: `typeof null` evaluates to `'object'`, so TypeScript retains `null` in the guarded branch.
cards.misconception: The typeof object guard excludes null during narrowing.

cards.statement: In the falsy branch of `if (s)`, `s: string | null` narrows to `null`.
cards.explanation: The empty string is falsy too, so TypeScript keeps `string | null` in the falsy branch. That is why a truthiness check on a string can skip `""`.
cards.misconception: A falsy check on a nullable string leaves only null.

cards.statement: When `x: string | number` equals `y: string | boolean`, both narrow to `string`.
cards.explanation: Inside an `x === y` branch, TypeScript keeps the type common to both unions. In this case, that common type is `string`.

cards.statement: For `x: number | null | undefined`, `x == null` narrows x to `null | undefined`.
cards.explanation: A loose equality comparison with `null` matches both `null` and `undefined`; TypeScript reflects that in the true branch.

cards.statement: The false branch of `'swim' in pet` removes variants with optional `swim`.
cards.explanation: A variant with optional `swim` remains possible on either side of an `in` check: the property may be present or absent.
cards.misconception: A failed in check excludes a union member that declares the checked property as optional.

cards.statement: For `class Foo { id = 1 }` and `const f: Foo = { id: 2 }`, `f instanceof Foo` is `true`.
cards.explanation: `instanceof` checks whether `Foo.prototype` is on the prototype chain of `f`, so the plain object literal fails it, even though TypeScript accepts it as a `Foo` by its shape.
cards.misconception: A value the checker accepts as a class type is an instance of that class at runtime.

cards.statement: An `x is Fish` return type narrows `Fish | Bird` at the call site.
cards.explanation: A function returning the type predicate `x is Fish` narrows a compatible argument to `Fish` in a branch where the call returns true.

cards.statement: An `asserts x is string` function narrows x after a successful call.
cards.explanation: After a call to an assertion function returns normally, TypeScript treats the asserted argument as the specified type for subsequent code.

cards.statement: A union with distinct literal `kind` values narrows by comparing `kind`.
cards.explanation: When each union member has a different literal value for a shared `kind` property, checking that property identifies the matching member.

cards.statement: After returning from a `typeof x === 'number'` branch, `string | number` x stays a union.
cards.explanation: The number path has returned and cannot reach the remaining code. TypeScript's control flow analysis narrows `x` to `string` there.
cards.misconception: Narrowing applies only inside a guard and does not account for an early return.

cards.statement: Before narrowing, TypeScript accepts the call `x.indexOf("a")` on a value `x: string | string[]`.
cards.explanation: Every member of this union has an `indexOf` method that takes a string, so TypeScript permits the call on the union without narrowing first.

cards.statement: TypeScript accepts a `string | number` argument for a parameter of type `string`.
cards.explanation: A `string | number` value might be a number. TypeScript requires narrowing before passing that value where a `string` is expected.
cards.misconception: A union value is assignable to any one of its member types.

cards.statement: For `{ id: string } | { id: number }`, reading `id` gives `string | number`.
cards.explanation: Both union members expose `id`; a read can produce either member's property type.

cards.statement: `{ id: string } & { active: boolean }` accepts an object with just `id`.
cards.explanation: The intersection combines both object requirements. A value also needs the `active` property.
cards.misconception: An object intersection accepts a value satisfying either side.

cards.statement: In `{ id: string } & { id: number }`, `id` has type `never`.
cards.explanation: The intersected property would need to be both `string` and `number`; its resulting type is `never`.

cards.statement: TypeScript limits the `extends` clause of an `interface` declaration to a single base type.
cards.explanation: An interface can list several types after `extends`, separated by commas, and inherits the members of each, as in `interface ColorfulCircle extends Colorful, Circle {}`.
cards.misconception: Interface extension accepts one base type.

cards.statement: Two declarations of the same interface automatically combine their distinct properties.
cards.explanation: Interface declaration merging joins members from declarations with the same name into one interface.

cards.statement: When two `interface Doc` declarations merge, TypeScript tries the earlier declaration's overloads first in a call.
cards.explanation: For a merged interface, overload resolution tries the later declaration's overload group first, each group in its own order. Signatures with a single string literal parameter type go before the rest.
cards.misconception: Merged method overloads retain declaration order from earliest to latest.

cards.statement: A type alias for `string` creates a distinct assignability type.
cards.explanation: An alias is another name for its target type. `type UserId = string` remains assignable from an ordinary string.
cards.misconception: A type alias creates a nominally distinct type.

cards.statement: A call to `identity<T>(x: T): T` requires `T` in angle brackets.
cards.explanation: TypeScript can infer `T` from the value argument. An explicit type argument is optional when inference succeeds.
cards.misconception: Generic function calls require explicit type arguments.

cards.statement: A function instantiates its generic `T` with `new T()` inside the body.
cards.explanation: `T` names a type, not a runtime constructor. A generic factory receives a constructor value, such as a parameter typed `new () => T`.
cards.misconception: A generic type parameter is available as a constructor at runtime.

cards.statement: A `T extends { length: number }` constraint permits reading `.length` from `T`.
cards.explanation: The constraint guarantees a numeric `length` member for values of `T`, so the generic function body may read it.

cards.statement: In `K extends keyof T`, a key must belong to `T`'s properties.
cards.explanation: `keyof T` restricts `K` to keys of `T`; a key absent from that type fails the constraint.

cards.statement: An interface can put `<T>` on a call signature for calls with different argument types.
cards.explanation: A generic call signature declares its own type parameter, allowing the interface to describe a function that is generic at each call.

cards.statement: A static property of `class Box<T>` uses `T` as its declared type.
cards.explanation: A generic class's static members cannot use its type parameter. The class is generic over its instance side.
cards.misconception: A generic class type parameter is available to static members.

cards.statement: A defaulted type parameter fills in when inference finds no candidate.
cards.explanation: If inference cannot choose a type argument, TypeScript uses that parameter's declared default.

cards.statement: A `const` type parameter changes inference for a variable passed by name.
cards.explanation: The `const` modifier affects inference for literal expressions written at the call site. A previously declared variable retains its existing inferred type.
cards.misconception: Const type parameters retroactively give named arguments const-like inferred types.

cards.statement: `function first<T extends any[]>(a: T) { return a[0]; }` infers its return type as `T[number]`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript resolves `a[0]` through the `any[]` constraint in this function, so its inferred return type is `any`.
cards.misconception: Indexing a generic array constraint preserves the element type of each call.

cards.statement: For `filter<T, F extends (x: T) => boolean>`, callers can specify just `T` and infer `F`.
cards.explanation: With both parameters required, a caller supplying `T` explicitly also has to supply `F`. The extra parameter prevents partial specification in this signature.
cards.misconception: A call can explicitly provide one required type argument and infer the next one.

cards.statement: `keyof { id: string; active: boolean }` is `"id" | "active"`.
cards.explanation: `keyof` produces a union of the object type's property keys.

cards.statement: `keyof` reduces a string index signature to the `string` type.
cards.explanation: For a string index signature, `keyof` is `string | number`. Numeric property access also reaches string-keyed properties.
cards.misconception: A string index signature gives `keyof` exactly `string`.

cards.statement: For `let item: { id: number }`, `typeof item` in a type is `{ id: number }`.
cards.explanation: In a type position, `typeof item` queries the type of the variable rather than producing JavaScript's runtime type string.

cards.statement: `let ok: typeof check();` types `ok` as `check`'s return type.
cards.explanation: In a type position, `typeof` takes only identifiers and their properties, so the call is a syntax error. `ReturnType<typeof check>` gives the return type.
cards.misconception: A type query can take a function call and yield its result type.

cards.statement: `{ id: number; name: string }["id"]` is `number`.
cards.explanation: An indexed access type looks up the property's declared type; the `id` property is numeric.

cards.statement: Indexing an object type with a union of keys intersects the property types.
cards.explanation: An indexed access using a union of keys produces a union of the corresponding property types.
cards.misconception: Looking up several keys combines their value types with an intersection.

cards.statement: `string[][number]` produces the array element type `string`.
cards.explanation: Using `number` as the index type of an array retrieves the type of its elements.

cards.statement: For `A = "a" | "b"` and `N = "1" | "2"`, the template literal type `${A}-${N}` is `"a-1" | "b-2"`.
cards.explanation: Each interpolated union is cross multiplied with the others, so two two-member unions give four strings: `"a-1" | "a-2" | "b-1" | "b-2"`.
cards.misconception: Template literal types zip union members by their positions.

cards.statement: `Capitalize<"hello world">` is `"Hello World"`.
cards.explanation: `Capitalize<"hello world">` produces `"Hello world"`; it changes the string's first character, not each word.
cards.misconception: Capitalize performs title casing across words.

cards.statement: `boolean extends true ? 1 : 2` resolves to the type `2`.
cards.explanation: `boolean` is the union `true | false`, and that union as a whole is not assignable to `true`, so the conditional type picks its false branch.

cards.statement: `T extends Array<infer Item> ? Item : T` extracts `number` from `number[]`.
cards.explanation: `infer Item` captures an array's element type when the array matches `Array<infer Item>`.

cards.statement: For `T = () => Promise<number>`, `T extends () => infer R ? R : never` is `number`.
cards.explanation: `infer R` in the return position captures the declared return type as a whole, so the result for `() => Promise<number>` is `Promise<number>`.
cards.misconception: Inferring a return type unwraps a returned promise.

cards.statement: `ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never` maps `string | number` to `string[] | number[]`.
cards.explanation: Because the conditional checks a generic type parameter, it distributes over the union and makes a separate array type for each member.

cards.statement: In `T extends { message: unknown } ? T["message"] : never`, the indexed access is valid.
cards.explanation: The true branch knows that `T` has a `message` property, so `T["message"]` is a valid indexed access there.

cards.statement: For `T = { id: 1; name: string }`, `{ [K in keyof T as Exclude<K, "id">]: T[K] }` keeps `id` as a `never` property.
cards.explanation: Producing `never` in the `as` clause filters the key out, so the result is `{ name: string }` with no `id` property at all.
cards.misconception: Remapping a key to never keeps the property and types it as never.

cards.statement: `[K in keyof T]+?` makes existing required properties optional.
cards.explanation: The `+?` mapping modifier adds optionality to generated properties. TypeScript also treats an unprefixed `?` as `+?`.

cards.statement: For `T = { a?: number; b: string }`, `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` is `{ b: string }`.
cards.explanation: The `-?` modifier removes the optional flag, not the property. Previously optional properties remain present and become required.
cards.misconception: Removing an optional modifier removes the property itself.

cards.statement: A mapped type's `as` clause controls its property value types.
cards.explanation: The `as` clause remaps generated property keys. The expression after the colon determines their value types.
cards.misconception: Mapped-type key remapping changes the property value types.

cards.statement: In `Required<Partial<{ id: number }>>`, `{}` fails assignment.
cards.explanation: Partial makes `id` optional, then Required makes it mandatory again; `{}` lacks the resulting required property.

cards.statement: `Readonly<{ config: { enabled: boolean } }>` makes the nested `enabled` property readonly.
cards.explanation: Readonly changes top-level properties. In this type, `config` cannot be reassigned, but its nested `enabled` property can.
cards.misconception: Readonly recursively freezes nested properties.

cards.statement: `Record<"a" | "b", number>` requires both `a` and `b` keys.
cards.explanation: `Record<"a" | "b", number>` creates a required numeric property for each key in its key union.

cards.statement: Given `string | 0 | null`, `NonNullable` filters out the literal member `0`.
cards.explanation: NonNullable removes `null` and `undefined`, not other falsy values. `NonNullable<string | 0 | null>` remains `string | 0`.
cards.misconception: NonNullable filters every falsy union member.

cards.statement: `Parameters` and `ReturnType` use an overloaded function’s first signature.
cards.explanation: For an overloaded function, both `Parameters<Type>` and `ReturnType<Type>` use the last overload signature.
cards.misconception: Utility types inspect the first overload signature.

cards.statement: For `class C { constructor(a: number, b?: string) {} }`, `ConstructorParameters<typeof C>` is `[a: number, b?: string]`.
cards.explanation: `ConstructorParameters` reads the parameter list of a constructor type such as `typeof C`, keeping each parameter's name and optional marker.

cards.statement: `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` produces `Promise<number>` after one level of unwrapping.
cards.explanation: Awaited recursively unwraps nested promises, so `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` is `number`.
cards.misconception: Awaited unwraps just one Promise layer.

cards.statement: `NoInfer<C>` lets a fallback value widen the `C` inferred from a separate `colors: C[]` argument.
cards.explanation: `NoInfer<C>` blocks the fallback from contributing inference candidates for `C`. The fallback is checked against `C` inferred from the other argument.
cards.misconception: A NoInfer parameter can widen the inferred type argument.

cards.statement: In an object context typed as `M & ThisType<{ x: number }>`, methods see `this.x` as `number`.
cards.explanation: `ThisType<{ x: number }>` marks the contextual `this` type for methods of a suitably typed object; `noImplicitThis` must be enabled.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = 4, B }`, TypeScript assigns `E.B` the numeric value `5`.
cards.explanation: A numeric enum member after a constant numeric member auto-increments the preceding value, so `B` is `5`.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = Math.random(), B }`, TypeScript automatically gives `B` the next value.
cards.explanation: An enum member following a computed initializer needs its own initializer. `B` in this declaration produces an error.
cards.misconception: A computed numeric enum member allows the next member to auto-increment.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = "a", B = A }`, TypeScript assigns `E.B` the string value `"a"`.
cards.explanation: A string enum member can initialize from another string enum member, so `B` receives `A`'s value, `"a"`.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = "a" }`, `E["a"]` yields the member name `"A"`.
cards.explanation: String enum members get no reverse mapping. The generated enum object has no `"a"` key mapped to `"A"`.
cards.misconception: String enums have the same reverse mapping as numeric enums.

cards.statement: For `enum E { A, B }`, TypeScript treats `E.A` and `E.B` as overlapping types.
cards.explanation: For a union enum with distinct literal members, `E.A` and `E.B` are disjoint member types; TypeScript flags impossible comparisons between them.
cards.misconception: Distinct literal enum members overlap in the checker.

cards.statement: `const enum E { A = 1 }` inlines `E.A` as a value in emitted JavaScript.
cards.explanation: A `const enum` is removed on emit, and references to its members are replaced with their constant values.

cards.statement: With `isolatedModules`, code can reference ambient `const enum` members.
cards.explanation: An ambient `const enum` has no emitted value, and `isolatedModules` rejects member references because single-file transpilation cannot inline them.
cards.misconception: Ambient const enums work with isolatedModules.

cards.statement: In `enum E { A = 0, B = "b" }`, TypeScript accepts both members.
cards.explanation: TypeScript permits an enum to mix numeric and string members. `A` is numeric and `B` is a string member in this declaration.

cards.statement: With `erasableSyntaxOnly` enabled, TypeScript accepts a regular `enum` declaration.
cards.explanation: `erasableSyntaxOnly` rejects regular enums because they require runtime code generation rather than simple type erasure.
cards.misconception: Enums are erasable TypeScript syntax.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `strict` is enabled by default.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 6.0 changed the `strict` default to `true`, and TypeScript 7.0 retains that default.

cards.statement: The `strict` family includes `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
cards.explanation: The `strict` family enables alwaysStrict, noImplicitAny, noImplicitThis, strictBindCallApply, strictBuiltinIteratorReturn, strictFunctionTypes, strictNullChecks, strictPropertyInitialization, and useUnknownInCatchVariables.
cards.misconception: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled by strict.

cards.statement: With `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, a built-in iterator’s return type parameter becomes `undefined`.
cards.explanation: `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn` gives built-in iterators `TReturn` of `undefined` instead of `any`.

cards.statement: With `strictFunctionTypes`, method parameters receive the same check as function property parameters.
cards.explanation: `strictFunctionTypes` applies the stricter parameter check to function syntax, but method syntax remains bivariant.
cards.misconception: strictFunctionTypes applies identically to methods and function properties.

cards.statement: With `strictPropertyInitialization`, `class C { x: string; constructor() {} }` reports an error.
cards.explanation: `strictPropertyInitialization` reports `x` because a required `string` field has neither a property initializer nor an assignment in the constructor.

cards.statement: With `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, TypeScript rejects an explicit `catch (e: any)` annotation.
cards.explanation: The flag changes only the type of an unannotated catch variable to `unknown`. An explicit `: any` annotation stays allowed and opts that catch clause out of the stricter type.
cards.misconception: The flag forbids any as a catch variable annotation.

cards.statement: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `obj["x"]` has type `string | undefined` when `obj: Record<string, string>`.
cards.explanation: When a key is present only via an index signature, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` includes `undefined` in the read type to account for a missing value.

cards.statement: With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `{ p: undefined }` fits `{ p?: string }`.
cards.explanation: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes an absent property from one holding `undefined`; `{ p: undefined }` fails against `{ p?: string }`.
cards.misconception: An optional property implicitly accepts an explicit undefined value under exactOptionalPropertyTypes.

cards.statement: Under `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, `settings.speed` errors when `speed` is declared beside an index signature.
cards.explanation: Properties declared in the type keep dot access. The flag only rejects dot access to keys that come from the index signature, which then need `settings["key"]`.
cards.misconception: The flag forces bracket access on every property of a type that has an index signature.

cards.statement: With `module: nodenext`, a `.ts` file’s module format follows the nearest `package.json` `type` field.
cards.explanation: `module: nodenext` selects ESM for a `.ts` file when the nearest package.json has `"type": "module"`; otherwise that file is CommonJS.

cards.statement: With `moduleResolution: bundler`, relative ESM imports require explicit `.js` extensions.
cards.explanation: `moduleResolution: bundler` supports extensionless relative imports, matching common bundler resolution behavior.
cards.misconception: Bundler resolution requires extensions for ESM relative imports.

cards.statement: With `module: preserve`, TypeScript converts `import = require` into an ESM import in emitted code.
cards.explanation: `module: preserve` keeps each import or export syntax: `import x = require("mod")` emits a `require` call, while ESM imports stay ESM.
cards.misconception: module preserve rewrites CommonJS imports as ESM imports.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `module` defaults to `esnext`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 6.0 switched the default `module` value to `esnext`, and TypeScript 7.0 kept it.

cards.statement: In TypeScript 7.0, `moduleResolution: node10` can be selected in `tsconfig.json`.
cards.explanation: TypeScript 7.0 rejects `moduleResolution: node10` as a removed option; use `nodenext` or `bundler` instead.
cards.misconception: node10 remains a supported module resolution strategy in TypeScript 7.0.

cards.statement: With `verbatimModuleSyntax`, TypeScript retains `import type` declarations in JavaScript output.
cards.explanation: `verbatimModuleSyntax` drops `import type` declarations from JavaScript output; imports lacking a `type` modifier remain.
cards.misconception: verbatimModuleSyntax preserves type-only imports in JavaScript.

cards.statement: With `isolatedModules`, `export { T }` triggers an error when `T` refers only to a type.
cards.explanation: `isolatedModules` reports value-style exports of names that refer only to types because a single-file transpiler cannot know whether those names exist at runtime.

cards.statement: When `baseUrl` is unset, TypeScript resolves `paths` targets relative to the tsconfig.json that declares them.
cards.explanation: Each `paths` target resolves relative to the tsconfig file itself when `baseUrl` is unset, so `paths` mappings work with no `baseUrl` in the configuration.

cards.statement: Since TypeScript 6.0, `types` includes visible `@types` packages by default.
cards.explanation: From TypeScript 6.0 onward, `types` defaults to `[]`. Visible `@types` packages enter the global scope when selected in `types`.
cards.misconception: All installed @types packages are automatically included in the global scope by default.

cards.statement: With `skipLibCheck`, TypeScript reports errors in a `.ts` file that misuses a type declared in a `.d.ts` file.
cards.explanation: `skipLibCheck` skips type checking inside declaration files, but TypeScript still checks your source code against the types those files declare.

cards.statement: A `declare global` block inside a module can extend a global interface.
cards.explanation: Global augmentation lets a module add to global declarations, such as the `Array` interface; it follows the same merge rules as module augmentation.
